claims.source: Crucially, for the red and green stimuli that were chosen to have equal absolute L-M contrast, the induced gamma-power change was not statistically different between the two (Figure 3E, red: 30.8%, CI95% = [20.3%, 43.5%], green: 31.2%, CI95% = [21.2%, 42.2%], t(29) = 0.135, pHolm = 0.89, BF01 = 7.0).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The data are 7.0 times more likely to occur under a hypothesis of no differences between red and green stimuli compared to a hypothesis assuming differences.
claims.source: The Bayes factor can be interpreted as meaning that the data are 7.0 times more likely to occur under a hypothesis of no differences between red and green stimuli compared to a hypothesis assuming differences.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical interpretation of the Bayes factor from the experimental data.

claims.claim: On the S-(L+M) axis, stimuli with equal absolute cone contrasts showed differing induced gamma power.
claims.source: On the S-(L+M) axis, stimuli with equal absolute cone contrasts showed differing induced gamma power: While yellow stimuli induced a 15.4% gamma-power increase over baseline (CI95% = [10.7%, 21.9%]), blue stimuli showed significantly smaller, very weak increases of only 2.2% (CI95% = [0.3%, 4.3%], t(29) = 4.02, pdifference < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claims.claim: Yellow stimuli induced a 15.4% gamma-power increase over baseline.
claims.source: On the S-(L+M) axis, stimuli with equal absolute cone contrasts showed differing induced gamma power: While yellow stimuli induced a 15.4% gamma-power increase over baseline (CI95% = [10.7%, 21.9%]), blue stimuli showed significantly smaller, very weak increases of only 2.2% (CI95% = [0.3%, 4.3%], t(29) = 4.02, pdifference < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Blue stimuli showed significantly smaller, very weak increases of only 2.2% gamma power over baseline.
claims.source: On the S-(L+M) axis, stimuli with equal absolute cone contrasts showed differing induced gamma power: While yellow stimuli induced a 15.4% gamma-power increase over baseline (CI95% = [10.7%, 21.9%]), blue stimuli showed significantly smaller, very weak increases of only 2.2% (CI95% = [0.3%, 4.3%], t(29) = 4.02, pdifference < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claims.claim: After regressing out per participant, per color, the N70 slope and amplitude from the induced gamma power, the induced gamma-power change residuals were not statistically different between red and green stimuli.
claims.source: To attempt to control for potential remaining differences in input drive that the DKL normalization missed, we regressed out per participant, per color, the N70 slope and amplitude from the induced gamma power. Results remained equivalent along the L-M axis: The induced gamma-power change residuals were not statistically different between red and green stimuli (red: 8.22, CI95% = [−0.42, 16.85], green: 12.09, CI95% = [5.44, 18.75], t(29) = 1.35, pHolm = 1.0, BF01 = 3.00).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claims.claim: Lower levels of input drive generated by equicontrast blue versus yellow stimuli might explain the weaker gamma oscillations induced by them.
claims.source: While blue stimuli still showed weaker gamma-power change residuals than yellow stimuli when regressing out changes in N70 slope and amplitude (blue: −11.23, CI95% = [−16.89, −5.57], yellow: −6.35, CI95% = [−11.20, −1.50]), this difference did not reach significance (t(29) = 1.65, pHolm = 0.88). This suggests that lower levels of input drive generated by equicontrast blue versus yellow stimuli might explain the weaker gamma oscillations induced by them.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Higher change-detection performance was correlated with stronger average V1 dipole moment across colors, in the time period from 67- to 93-ms poststimulus onset.
claims.source: Higher change-detection performance (defined as lower final staircased target color contrast) was correlated with stronger average V1 dipole moment (i.e., the negative ERF amplitude during the N70 component) across colors, in the time period from 67- to 93-ms poststimulus onset (Figure 4A, rmax = 0.43, all pTmax < 0.03, corrected for multiple comparisons across time).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Higher change-detection performance was correlated with stronger induced V1 power across colors, for several gamma frequency ranges.
claims.source: Higher change-detection performance was also correlated with stronger induced V1 power across colors, for several gamma frequency ranges (Figure 4B; at 34–37 Hz: rmax = −0.27, all pTmax ≤ 0.03; at 39–40 Hz: rmax = −0.23, all pTmax < 0.04; at 44–53 Hz: rmax = −0.31, all pTmax ≤ 0.03, corrected for multiple comparisons across frequency).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: There were significant correlations between the N70 ERF component and induced gamma power.
claims.source: In addition, there were significant correlations between the N70 ERF component and induced gamma power: The extracted N70 amplitude was correlated across colors with the induced gamma-power change within participants with on average r = −0.38 (CI95% = [−0.49, −0.28], pWilcoxon < 4 × 10−6).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claims.claim: The correlation between N70 ERF component and induced gamma power was specific to the gamma band and the N70 component.
claims.source: This correlation was specific to the gamma band and the N70 component: Across colors, there were significant correlation clusters between V1 dipole moment 68- to 79-ms poststimulus onset and induced power between 28–54 and 72 Hz (Figure 4C, rmax = −0.30, pTmax < 0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons across time and frequency).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: When perceptual definitions of equiluminance are used, there is substantial between-subject variability in the ratio of relative L- and M-cone contributions to perceived luminance, with a mean ratio of L/M luminance contributions of 1.5–2.3.
claims.source: When perceptual (instead of neuronal) definitions of equiluminance are used, there is substantial between-subject variability in the ratio of relative L- and M-cone contributions to perceived luminance, with a mean ratio of L/M luminance contributions of 1.5–2.3 (He et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: The ratio of color change-detection performance between red and green (L divided by M) had an average value of 1.48, with substantial variability over subjects.
claims.source: Our perceptual results are consistent with that: We had determined the color-contrast change-detection threshold per color; We used the inverse of this threshold as a metric of color change-detection performance; The ratio of this performance metric between red and green (L divided by M) had an average value of 1.48, with substantial variability over subjects (CI95% = [1.33, 1.66]).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Change-detection threshold red/green ratios were neither correlated with ERF N70 amplitude red/green ratios nor with induced gamma-power red/green ratios.
claims.source: If such variability also affected the neuronal ERF and gamma-power measures reported here, L/M-ratios in color-contrast change-detection thresholds should be correlated with L/M-ratios in ERF amplitude and induced gamma power across participants. This was not the case: Change-detection threshold red/green ratios were neither correlated with ERF N70 amplitude red/green ratios (ρ = 0.09, p = 0.65, BF01 = 3.99), nor with induced gamma-power red/green ratios (ρ = −0.17, p = 0.38, BF01 = 3.04).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claims.claim: Uniform colored stimuli induced gamma oscillations in humans that were measurable in MEG recordings, confirming a previous study.
claims.source: In summary, uniform colored stimuli induced gamma oscillations in humans that were measurable in MEG recordings, confirming a previous study (Perry et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data, supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: When red-green color hues were chosen to equalize cone contrast on the L-M axis, the induced V1 gamma power did not differ between red and green hues.
claims.source: When red-green color hues were chosen to equalize cone contrast on the L-M axis (and thereby to ideally equalize input drive), the induced V1 gamma power did not differ between red and green hues.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Pure activation of the S-(L+M) axis induced weaker gamma power, especially for color hues activating primarily the S-cone.
claims.source: Additionally, pure activation of the S-(L+M) axis induced weaker gamma power, especially for color hues activating primarily the S-cone.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis could be seen in smaller amplitudes of early ERF components (N70) in area V1 and in worse color-contrast change-detection performance for high-S (blue) stimuli.
claims.source: This curious asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis could also be seen in smaller amplitudes of early ERF components (N70) in area V1 and in worse color-contrast change-detection performance for high-S (blue) stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Across hues, N70 amplitude and gamma power were correlated with color-contrast change-detection performance.
claims.source: Accordingly, across hues, N70 amplitude and gamma power were correlated with color-contrast change-detection performance.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Controlling for N70 amplitude and slope strongly diminished the recorded differences in induced gamma power between S+ and S− stimuli.
claims.source: The fact that controlling for N70 amplitude and slope strongly diminished the recorded differences in induced gamma power between S+ and S− stimuli supports the idea that the recorded differences in induced gamma power over the S-(L+M) axis might be due to pure S+ stimuli generating weaker input drive to V1 compared to DKL-equicontrast S− stimuli, even when cone contrasts are equalized.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The recorded differences in induced gamma power over the S-(L+M) axis might be due to pure S+ stimuli generating weaker input drive to V1 compared to DKL-equicontrast S− stimuli, even when cone contrasts are equalized.
claims.source: The fact that controlling for N70 amplitude and slope strongly diminished the recorded differences in induced gamma power between S+ and S− stimuli supports the idea that the recorded differences in induced gamma power over the S-(L+M) axis might be due to pure S+ stimuli generating weaker input drive to V1 compared to DKL-equicontrast S− stimuli, even when cone contrasts are equalized.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The study found stronger gamma power and ERF N70 responses to stimuli along the green-yellow/red-blue axis compared to stimuli along the red-yellow/green-blue axis.
claims.source: Concerning off-axis colors (red-blue, green-blue, green-yellow, and red-yellow), we found stronger gamma power and ERF N70 responses to stimuli along the green-yellow/red-blue axis (which has been called lime-magenta in previous studies) compared to stimuli along the red-yellow/green-blue axis (orange-cyan).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: In human studies varying color contrast along these axes, lime-magenta has been found to induce stronger fMRI responses.
claims.source: In human studies varying color contrast along these axes, lime-magenta has also been found to induce stronger fMRI responses (Goddard et al., 2010; but see Lafer-Sousa et al., 2012), and psychophysical work has proposed a cortical color channel along this axis (Danilova and Mollon, 2010; but see Witzel and Gegenfurtner, 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Psychophysical work has proposed a cortical color channel along the lime-magenta axis.
claims.source: In human studies varying color contrast along these axes, lime-magenta has also been found to induce stronger fMRI responses (Goddard et al., 2010; but see Lafer-Sousa et al., 2012), and psychophysical work has proposed a cortical color channel along this axis (Danilova and Mollon, 2010; but see Witzel and Gegenfurtner, 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The color-induced gamma oscillation clearly localized to early visual cortex, was narrow-banded and showed (for 90% of subjects) a second spectral peak around 80–100 Hz.
claims.source: In our data, the color-induced gamma oscillation clearly localized to early visual cortex, was narrow-banded and showed (for 90% of subjects) a second spectral peak around 80–100 Hz, which did not seem to be a harmonic of the main induced peak and which was rare for grating stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The second spectral peak did not seem to be a harmonic of the main induced peak and was rare for grating stimuli.
claims.source: In our data, the color-induced gamma oscillation clearly localized to early visual cortex, was narrow-banded and showed (for 90% of subjects) a second spectral peak around 80–100 Hz, which did not seem to be a harmonic of the main induced peak and which was rare for grating stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The induced gamma-power change source-localized as a continuous source over the early visual cortex with a peak in V1.
claims.source: As the induced gamma-power change source-localized as a continuous source over the early visual cortex with a peak in V1, our data cannot differentiate between a strong gamma source in V1 that shows source smearing over neighboring areas and, alternatively, several gamma sources in V1–V4 that show monotonous decreases in power with distance from V1.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The data cannot differentiate between a strong gamma source in V1 that shows source smearing over neighboring areas and several gamma sources in V1–V4 that show monotonous decreases in power with distance from V1.
claims.source: As the induced gamma-power change source-localized as a continuous source over the early visual cortex with a peak in V1, our data cannot differentiate between a strong gamma source in V1 that shows source smearing over neighboring areas and, alternatively, several gamma sources in V1–V4 that show monotonous decreases in power with distance from V1.
claims.evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on their data.

claims.claim: Recruiting a bigger sample of human participants allowed the study to generalize findings of color gamma responses to the population level.
claims.source: While most previous studies of gamma responses to colored stimuli were limited to small samples of non-human primates or human patients, recruiting a bigger sample of human participants allowed us to generalize findings of color gamma responses to the population level (Fries and Maris, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological advantage claimed by the authors, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The MEG signal does not represent a simple average over all population activity underneath the MEG sensor, but is influenced by the location and orientation of the underlying neuronal dipoles and is most sensitive to synchronized neuronal activity.
claims.source: When comparing our results to previous reports based on intracranial recordings, it is important to note that the MEG signal does not represent a simple average over all population activity underneath the MEG sensor, but is influenced by the location and orientation of the underlying neuronal dipoles and is most sensitive to synchronized neuronal activity (Baillet, 2017; Murakami and Okada, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about MEG, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The total power reported in MEG does not correspond to the total power of all oscillatory neuronal activity in V1.
claims.source: Thereby, the total power reported here does not correspond to the total power of all oscillatory neuronal activity in V1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of MEG signals.

claims.claim: Activity sources that are of unequal frequency or phase are likely not fully captured in MEG recordings.
claims.source: Additionally, activity sources that are of unequal frequency or phase are likely not fully captured in MEG recordings.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of MEG signals.

claims.claim: Intracortical recordings will usually not sample all of area V1 equally, but will emphasize the color tuning of neuronal populations close to the electrodes.
claims.source: On the other hand, intracortical recordings will usually not sample all of area V1 equally, but will emphasize the color tuning of neuronal populations close to the electrodes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of intracortical recordings.

claims.claim: With careful head stabilization and exclusion of subjects showing excessive head movements, spatial resolution of source-localized MEG can be brought down to between 0.45 and 7 mm, depending on dipole location.
claims.source: The localization accuracy of source-localized MEG is limited by subject movement, uncertainties in head tracking and source spread. However, with careful head stabilization and exclusion of subjects showing excessive head movements (as practiced here), spatial resolution can be brought down to between 0.45 and 7 mm, depending on dipole location (Nasiotis et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: The high similarity between early (source-localized) V1 ERF components recorded in this study and intracortical V1 ERP components recorded in macaque suggests that V1-localized activity in MEG captures the underlying intracortical voltage signal in V1.
claims.source: Additionally, the high similarity between early (source-localized) V1 ERF components recorded here and intracortical V1 ERP components recorded in macaque (Rols et al., 2001) suggests that our V1-localized activity in MEG captures the underlying intracortical voltage signal in V1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous work, supported by citation.

claims.claim: In most previous studies analyzing early visual cortex gamma-band responses to colored stimuli, the presented colors were not equiluminant and did not have equal color contrasts to the background.
claims.source: In several previous studies in non-human and human primates analyzing early visual cortex gamma-band responses to colored stimuli, a red effect, that is stronger induced gamma power for red versus non-red colors, was reported. In most of these studies, the presented colors were not equiluminant and did not have equal color contrasts to the background.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' review of previous literature.

claims.claim: Rols et al., 2001 described stronger gamma power for a red stimulus compared to a green and a yellow one in anesthetized macaque V1 and V4.
claims.source: In an initial report on recordings in anesthetized macaque V1 and V4, Rols et al., 2001 first described stronger gamma power for a red stimulus compared to a green and a yellow one (heteroluminant, all presented on a gray background).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Color-induced gamma oscillations were significantly stronger in V1 than in V4 in the recordings by Rols et al., 2001.
claims.source: Similar to our study, color-induced gamma oscillations were significantly stronger in V1 than in V4 in their recordings.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to previous work, supported by implicit citation.

claims.claim: Shirhatti and Ray, 2018, recording in awake macaque V1, found strongest gamma power for red and blue hues.
claims.source: Shirhatti and Ray, 2018, recording in awake macaque V1, presented fullscreen, heteroluminant colors after a gray intertrial background and found strongest gamma power for red and blue hues.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: When colors were transformed to coordinates based on L- and M-cone activation, induced gamma power was found to increase with cone contrast modulations toward both axis directions in one of the three monkeys tested by Shirhatti and Ray, 2018.
claims.source: When colors were transformed to coordinates based on L- and M-cone activation, induced gamma power was found to increase with cone contrast modulations toward both axis directions in one of the three monkeys tested.
claims.evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Shirhatti and Ray, 2018.

claims.claim: Brunet et al., 2015 found that the strongest gamma power was induced by images of a colored orange on a gray background in ECoG recordings over awake macaque areas V1 and V4.
claims.source: Using natural stimuli, Brunet et al., 2015 presented 65 grayscale and color images to two macaque monkeys and found that, in ECoG recordings over awake macaque areas V1 and V4, the strongest gamma power was induced by images of a colored orange on a gray background.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: In another study of macaque V1 responses to natural stimuli, induced gamma power increased with both negative and positive L-M cone contrast.
claims.source: In another study of macaque V1 responses to natural stimuli, induced gamma power increased with both negative and positive L-M cone contrast (Peter et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Peter et al., 2019 found strongest gamma responses to pink and red stimuli in intracortical recordings from macaque V1 under visual stimulation with a peripheral colored disk.
claims.source: In intracortical recordings from macaque V1 under visual stimulation with a peripheral colored disk, Peter et al., 2019 found strongest gamma responses to pink and red stimuli.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: When colors were chosen from an equiluminance plane in DKL space for a control analysis in one monkey, Peter et al., 2019 still found slightly stronger gamma power for red than for green stimuli, even if red and green stimuli were of the same color contrast.
claims.source: When colors were chosen from an equiluminance plane in DKL space for a control analysis in one monkey, they still found slightly stronger gamma power for red than for green stimuli, even if red and green stimuli were of the same color contrast.
claims.evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Peter et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Peter et al., 2019 found the same asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis as reported in the current study, in the sense that pure blue stimuli induced very weak gamma power.
claims.source: The same asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis as reported here was found, in the sense that pure blue stimuli induced very weak gamma power.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to previous work, supported by implicit citation to Peter et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Peter et al., 2019 found that red induced the strongest gamma power only when presented on a gray background, but not when presented on a black background.
claims.source: In addition, they explored the effects of prestimulus and background adaptation and found that red induced the strongest gamma power only when presented on a gray background, but not when presented on a black background.
claims.evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Peter et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Peter et al., 2019 showed that red and green stimuli induce equal gamma power when the background does not adapt M- and L-cones.
claims.source: Presenting a series of different stimulus and background combinations and summarizing results in a self-defined cone adaptation model, they showed that red and green stimuli induce equal gamma power when the background does not adapt M- and L-cones, and that, over all stimulus/background combinations, M-cone-activating backgrounds boost L-cone-stimulus-driven gamma oscillations the strongest.
claims.evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Peter et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Peter et al., 2019 showed that M-cone-activating backgrounds boost L-cone-stimulus-driven gamma oscillations the strongest.
claims.source: Presenting a series of different stimulus and background combinations and summarizing results in a self-defined cone adaptation model, they showed that red and green stimuli induce equal gamma power when the background does not adapt M- and L-cones, and that, over all stimulus/background combinations, M-cone-activating backgrounds boost L-cone-stimulus-driven gamma oscillations the strongest.
claims.evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Peter et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Bartoli et al., 2019 found strongest gamma-power responses for full-screen red/orange stimuli following a gray intertrial interval background in recordings from ECoG electrodes implanted over areas V1–V4 in 10 epilepsy patients.
claims.source: In recordings from ECoG electrodes implanted over areas V1–V4 in 10 epilepsy patients, Bartoli et al., 2019 found strongest gamma-power responses for full-screen red/orange stimuli following a gray intertrial interval background.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: The presented colors in Bartoli et al., 2019 were equiluminant and equicontrast in CIELAB, a color coordinate system based on perceptual similarity.
claims.source: The presented colors were equiluminant and equicontrast in CIELAB, a color coordinate system based on perceptual similarity.
claims.evidence: This describes the methods of a previous study, supported by implicit citation to Bartoli et al., 2019.

claims.claim: In ECoG and intracranial EEG recordings from a second set of seven epilepsy patients using the same task and stimuli, Li et al., 2022 found strongest gamma-power responses for red/orange and green stimuli.
claims.source: In ECoG and intracranial EEG recordings from a second set of seven epilepsy patients using the same task and stimuli (Li et al., 2022), strongest gamma-power responses were found for red/orange and green stimuli.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: Color gamma responses reported in Bartoli et al., 2019 and Li et al., 2022 were of similar strength (expressed in percent change from baseline) as in the current MEG study.
claims.source: Color gamma responses reported in both studies were of similar strength (expressed in percent change from baseline) as in our MEG study.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to previous work, supported by implicit citations.

claims.claim: Perry et al., 2020 reported oscillatory neuronal responses to full-screen colored stimuli in MEG recordings from 20 participants.
claims.source: Oscillatory neuronal responses to full-screen colored stimuli have also been reported in MEG recordings from 20 participants (Perry et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: When full-screen red, green, purple, and blue colors were shown after a gray background or in alteration, red stimuli induced the strongest power in several oscillatory bands above 30 Hz in Perry et al., 2020.
claims.source: When full-screen red, green, purple, and blue colors were shown after a gray background or in alteration, red stimuli induced the strongest power in several oscillatory bands above 30 Hz.
claims.evidence: Supported by implicit citation to Perry et al., 2020.

claims.claim: All previous studies not explicitly controlling for cone contrast found stronger gamma-power responses for red (and sometimes blue) stimuli than for other colors.
claims.source: In total, all previous studies not explicitly controlling for cone contrast found stronger gamma-power responses for red (and sometimes blue) stimuli than for other colors.
claims.evidence: This is a summary inference based on the authors' review of previous literature.

claims.claim: When cone contrast was controlled for in two macaque V1 studies, the difference between red and green stimuli either decreased or disappeared.
claims.source: When cone contrast was controlled for in two macaque V1 studies, either through the use of DKL coordinates or through a self-defined cone adaption model, the difference between red and green stimuli either decreased (Peter et al., 2019; Shirhatti and Ray, 2018) or, when adaptation was also taken into account, disappeared (Peter et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of previous work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Macaque V1 glucose uptake, intrinsic signal imaging and 2-photon calcium imaging found strongest responses for the employed red and blue stimuli.
claims.source: Interestingly, a similar case has been found before in other measures of V1 activation: Macaque V1 glucose uptake, intrinsic signal imaging and 2-photon calcium imaging found strongest responses for the employed red and blue stimuli (Garg et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Tootell et al., 1988; Xiao et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: End-spectral biases in V1 activation measures were likely at least partially an effect of the respective stimulus presentation and color coordinate systems.
claims.source: These so-called end-spectral biases were likely at least partially an effect of the respective stimulus presentation and color coordinate systems, insofar as their red and blue colors induced maximal cone contrasts in the L-M pathway – highest L-M excitation for their red stimuli, and highest L excitation for their blue stimuli (Li et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Mollon, 2009; Valverde Salzmann et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on previous work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Compared to L- and M-cones, S-cones are sparser.
claims.source: This asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis might be driven by underlying physiology: Compared to L- and M-cones, S-cones are sparser (DeMonasterio et al., 1981) and show slower light responses, higher noise levels, and higher activation thresholds (Baudin et al., 2019; Cole et al., 1993; Lee et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: S-cones show slower light responses, higher noise levels, and higher activation thresholds compared to L- and M-cones.
claims.source: This asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis might be driven by underlying physiology: Compared to L- and M-cones, S-cones are sparser (DeMonasterio et al., 1981) and show slower light responses, higher noise levels, and higher activation thresholds (Baudin et al., 2019; Cole et al., 1993; Lee et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: S-(L+M)-sensitive neurons are sparser than L-M-sensitive ones in the LGN.
claims.source: Additionally, S-(L+M)-sensitive neurons are sparser than L-M-sensitive ones in the LGN (Derrington et al., 1984) and V1 (Li et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: S-(L+M)-sensitive neurons are sparser than L-M-sensitive ones in V1.
claims.source: Additionally, S-(L+M)-sensitive neurons are sparser than L-M-sensitive ones in the LGN (Derrington et al., 1984) and V1 (Li et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Within V1, neurons sensitive to S-cone inputs reside in different cortical layers and respond later than other color-sensitive neurons.
claims.source: Within V1, neurons sensitive to S-cone inputs reside in different cortical layers and respond later than other color-sensitive neurons (Cottaris and De Valois, 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claims.claim: S-cone-induced signals are comparatively weak within LGN and are amplified and transformed in V1.
claims.source: Likely, S-cone-induced signals are comparatively weak within LGN and are amplified and transformed in V1 (De Valois et al., 2000; Mullen et al., 2008; Xiao, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on previous work, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Stimuli high and low on the S-(L+M) axis (S+ and S−) each target different cell populations in the LGN.
claims.source: Contrary to the unified pathway for L-M activation, stimuli high and low on the S-(L+M) axis (S+ and S−) each target different cell populations in the LGN, and different cortical layers within V1 (Chatterjee and Callaway, 2003; De Valois et al., 2000), whereby the S+ pathway shows higher LGN neuron and V1 afferent input numbers (Chatterjee and Callaway, 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Stimuli high and low on the S-(L+M) axis (S+ and S−) each target different cortical layers within V1.

claims.claim: Color-induced gamma responses in area V1 match LGN-to-V1 input strength in three measured aspects.

results.result: The study used MEG to record gamma oscillations in 30 human participants viewing equiluminant color stimuli with equalized cone contrasts in DKL space. Source-localized analysis revealed that color-induced gamma responses localized to early visual cortex with a peak in V1, demonstrating that color gamma responses can be studied non-invasively in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C38-C42 collectively describe the experimental design and primary localization finding. The methods are clearly described (equiluminant stimuli, DKL space, n=30, MEG recording), and the localization to V1 is supported by source-level analysis with appropriate citations to beamforming methods. This is a core methodological and technical validation result.

results.result: When red and green stimuli were equalized for L-M cone contrast in DKL space, induced gamma power in V1 did not differ between the two colors. Statistical analysis including Bayes factor (BF01=7.0) supports the absence of a red bias when cone contrast is properly controlled.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C11-C12, C43-C44, C81-C82, and C96 converge on the primary finding that contradicts previous reports of red bias. The statistical support is strong (t-test p=0.89, BF01=7.0), and the experimental design explicitly controlled for the confound identified in prior work. This directly addresses the study's main hypothesis.

results.result: Blue stimuli on the S-cone axis induced very weak gamma responses (2.2% increase), significantly smaller event-related fields, and poorer change-detection performance compared to other colors, particularly yellow stimuli (15.4% gamma increase).
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C45, C83-C85, and C97 describe converging evidence for weak S-cone responses across multiple measures (gamma power, ERF amplitude, behavioral performance). Statistical support is provided (t(29)=4.02, p<0.001), and the pattern is consistent across neural and behavioral metrics. This represents a robust secondary finding.

results.result: After regressing out N70 ERF slope and amplitude to control for input drive differences, the gamma power difference between red and green stimuli remained non-significant (BF01=3.00), while the blue-yellow difference was diminished though not eliminated, suggesting that weaker S-cone input drive may partially explain the asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 and C100-C101 describe a control analysis attempting to account for input drive differences. While the L-M axis result is strengthened (BF01=3.00), the S-(L+M) axis result becomes non-significant (p=0.88) after correction, making the interpretation speculative (C87, C101 are marked as speculation). The analysis is appropriate but the conclusion about S-cone input drive remains tentative.

results.result: Across color hues, higher change-detection performance correlated with stronger N70 ERF amplitude (67-93 ms, rmax=0.43, p<0.03) and stronger induced gamma power (34-53 Hz ranges). N70 amplitude and gamma power were also correlated with each other (r=-0.38, p<4×10⁻⁶), specifically in the gamma band and N70 time window.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 and C99 describe correlational relationships between behavioral performance, ERF, and gamma power. Statistical support is provided with appropriate multiple comparison corrections (tmax correction). The specificity to gamma band and N70 component (C91) strengthens the interpretation. These correlations support the link between input drive and gamma power.

results.result: Participants achieved ~85% accuracy on the change-detection task as intended by the staircase procedure. However, detection thresholds varied significantly across hues (F(7,203)=82.18, p<3×10⁻¹⁶), with blue stimuli requiring exceptionally high contrast changes (71%) compared to other colors (20-37%). Reaction times also differed across hues (F(7,203)=9.26, p<7×10⁻¹⁰), being fastest for red (509 ms) and slowest for green-yellow (562 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C54 describe behavioral results with strong statistical support. The staircase successfully achieved target accuracy, and the hue-dependent differences in thresholds and reaction times are well-documented with appropriate statistics. The blue outlier is particularly notable and consistent with the neural findings.

results.result: Both grating and color stimuli induced clear V1 ERFs with an N70 component (57-94 ms) that differed significantly across stimuli (F(3.48,101.04)=30.32, p<3×10⁻¹⁵). The N70 was stronger for gratings than colors and strongest for red/green-yellow colors but weakest for blue. N70 slope was significantly shallower for blue compared to other hues, demonstrating approximately equalized stimulus drive across all hues except blue. N70 peak latency was significantly delayed for blue stimuli (88.6 ms) compared to red (77.9 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C65 describe comprehensive ERF characterization with robust statistical support. The N70 component is well-characterized across amplitude, slope, and latency measures. The finding that stimulus drive was equalized except for blue (C62) is critical for interpreting the gamma results. Multiple pairwise comparisons with Holm correction strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Color and grating stimuli induced significant narrowband gamma power increases in early visual cortex, strongest in V1-V4. Color stimuli induced 19% gamma power increases while gratings induced 100% increases (tdifference(29)=8.32, p<4×10⁻⁹). Ninety-seven percent of participants showed significant gamma peaks for at least one color and the grating. Notably, 90% of participants showed a second higher gamma peak (~80-100 Hz) for color stimuli, but only 13% showed this for gratings.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C73 describe the basic gamma response characteristics with strong statistical support and high prevalence across participants. The differential presence of a second peak for colors vs. gratings (C72-C73) is a novel observation. Source localization to V1-V4 is well-documented. These findings establish the basic phenomenon under investigation.

results.result: For color stimuli, the frequently observed second gamma peak (80-100 Hz) showed no linear relationship with the first peak frequency (r=0.06, p=0.58), indicating it was unlikely to be a harmonic. This second peak was rare for grating stimuli, suggesting differences in underlying circuits or dynamics between chromatic and achromatic processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 and C105-C106 describe the characterization of the second gamma peak with appropriate statistical testing. The lack of correlation rules out the harmonic hypothesis. However, the mechanistic interpretation about different circuits (C106, C152) remains speculative. The observation itself is well-supported.

results.result: The lower gamma peak frequency differed significantly between grating (51.6 Hz) and color stimuli (45.9 Hz, p<3×10⁻³), and these frequencies were correlated across participants (r=0.64, p<3×10⁻⁴). However, gamma peak frequencies did not differ significantly between different color pairs (all pHolm>0.36), indicating roughly equalized input drive across colors. The higher gamma peak (~96-97 Hz) showed no differences between grating and colors or across different colors.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 describe gamma peak frequency characteristics with appropriate statistical support. The lack of frequency differences across colors (C78) supports the interpretation of equalized input drive (C79), which is critical for the main conclusions. The correlation between grating and color peak frequencies (C77) suggests common mechanisms.

results.result: The ratio of color change-detection performance between red and green (L/M = 1.48, CI95%=[1.33,1.66]) was consistent with known perceptual variability in L/M luminance contributions (1.5-2.3). However, these behavioral L/M ratios were not correlated with ERF N70 amplitude ratios (ρ=0.09, p=0.65, BF01=3.99) or gamma power ratios (ρ=-0.17, p=0.38, BF01=3.04) across participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 describe an important control analysis testing whether perceptual variability affects the neural measures. The lack of correlation (with Bayes factors supporting the null) strengthens the conclusion that the neural equalization of red/green responses is not confounded by individual differences in perceptual equiluminance. This is a critical validation.

results.result: Off-axis colors along the lime-magenta (green-yellow/red-blue) axis showed stronger gamma power and ERF N70 responses compared to the orange-cyan (red-yellow/green-blue) axis. This is consistent with previous fMRI findings and psychophysical proposals of a cortical color channel along the lime-magenta axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 describe an observation about off-axis colors with support from prior literature. However, the current study's data supporting this claim (C102) is not quantified with statistics in the provided text. The consistency with prior work (C103-C104) provides convergent validity, but the strength of evidence from the current data alone is unclear.

results.result: The induced gamma power source-localized as a continuous source over early visual cortex with a peak in V1. However, the data cannot differentiate between a strong V1 source with spatial smearing versus multiple sources in V1-V4 with monotonous power decreases from V1.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 acknowledge an important limitation of the source localization method. This is an appropriate and honest assessment of what can and cannot be concluded from MEG source localization. The limitation does not undermine the main findings but appropriately qualifies the spatial interpretation.

results.result: Recruiting 30 participants allowed population-level generalization beyond small primate samples. MEG signals are sensitive to synchronized activity and influenced by dipole location/orientation, not representing total V1 activity. With careful head stabilization, MEG spatial resolution can reach 0.45-7 mm. The similarity between MEG V1 ERFs and macaque intracortical V1 ERPs suggests MEG captures underlying V1 voltage signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C115 discuss methodological considerations and advantages of the MEG approach. The sample size advantage (C109) is valid for population generalization. The discussion of MEG limitations (C110-C113) is appropriate and well-cited. The spatial resolution claim (C114) and validation against macaque data (C115) are supported by citations. These are important methodological points.

results.result: Prior work established that color surfaces induce gamma oscillations in primate V1, with particularly strong responses reported for red stimuli. However, previous studies often did not control for precortical color processing and V1 input strength. The DKL color space, based on LGN cone contrast axes (L+M, L-M, S-(L+M)), provides a framework for equalizing input drive. Individual variability in cone sensitivity necessitates larger sample sizes for population-level conclusions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C37 establish the background and rationale for the study. These are well-supported by extensive citations to prior literature. The identification of the confound in prior work (C3-C4) is the key motivation. The DKL framework (C30-C32) is established knowledge. The rationale for sample size (C36-C37) is sound. This provides essential context but is not a result of the current study.

results.result: Review of previous studies shows that most reports of stronger gamma for red stimuli did not control for cone contrast. When cone contrast was controlled in macaque V1 studies, the red-green difference either decreased or disappeared. Similar end-spectral biases have been observed in other V1 activation measures (glucose uptake, intrinsic imaging, calcium imaging), likely due to maximal cone contrasts in the stimulus presentation systems used.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C136 provide a comprehensive review of prior literature, identifying the pattern that cone contrast control eliminates or reduces the red bias. This is well-supported by multiple citations and provides critical context for interpreting the current findings. The synthesis across different measurement modalities (C137-C138) strengthens the argument. This is scholarly review, not original data.

results.result: The asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis may be driven by underlying physiology: S-cones are sparser, slower, noisier, and have higher thresholds than L/M-cones. S-(L+M)-sensitive neurons are sparser in LGN and V1, reside in different cortical layers, and respond later. Despite more numerous S+ inputs to V1, ERPs/ERFs show weaker and delayed responses. The results suggest cortical gamma is more closely related to ERP/ERF processes than to input numerosity.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C149 synthesize known physiology (C139-C147, well-cited) with the current findings (C148-C149) to explain the S-cone asymmetry. The physiological basis is well-established in prior literature. The interpretation linking gamma to ERF rather than input numerosity (C149) is supported by the correlation data (C88-C91) and the regression analysis (C100). This is a well-reasoned mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Color-induced gamma responses in V1 match LGN-to-V1 input strength in three aspects: (1) equal gamma for equal L-M cone contrast stimuli, (2) diminished gamma for S-cone stimuli with weaker LGN input, and (3) correlation between N70 amplitude and gamma power. These findings suggest common principles for chromatic and achromatic gamma generation, though the second gamma peak for colors suggests some differences. Previous reports of color specificity may be explained by the positive relationship between feedforward input strength and gamma power.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C154 synthesize the main findings into a coherent mechanistic framework. The three-point summary (C153) accurately captures the key results. The interpretation of common principles (C151) is supported by the data, though the caveat about differences (C152) is appropriately speculative. The explanation of prior findings (C154) is a reasonable inference but remains somewhat speculative. This is a strong integrative conclusion.

results.result: The study recruited 30 participants (18 female, age 18-36, mean 26) from the general public based on MEG field standards. Five additional subjects were excluded for equipment malfunctions or excessive movement (>5 mm). The study was approved by the ethics committee of Goethe University Frankfurt.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C159 describe basic methodological details about participants and ethics approval. These are straightforward factual statements about the study design. The sample size justification (C155) is appropriate for the field. The exclusion criteria (C158) are reasonable and clearly stated. This is standard methodological reporting.

results.result: In summary, uniform colored stimuli induced gamma oscillations measurable in MEG, confirming prior work. The asymmetry on the S-(L+M) axis was evident in smaller N70 ERF amplitudes and worse change-detection performance for blue stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C95 and C98 are summary statements that accurately reflect the findings described in other claim groups. C95 confirms the basic phenomenon (supported by C66-C73, C95), and C98 summarizes the S-cone findings (supported by C8-C10, C58-C59, C49). These are valid summary statements of well-supported results.
